Introduction
This section presents an assessment of potential water quality impacts arising from
construction and operation of the Project, which has been conducted in accordance
with the criteria and guidelines for evaluating and assessing water pollution as stated
in Annex 6 and Annex 14 of the "Technical Memorandum on Environmental Impact
Assessment Process" (EIAO-TM) as well as the requirements given in Clause 3.5.5
and Appendix D of the EIA Study Brief (No. ESB-375/2025) (hereinafter "the Study
Brief").
Environmental Legislation, Standards and Guidelines
Technical Memorandum on Environmental Impact Assessment Ordinance (EIAO-
TM)
The EIAO-TM was issued by EPD under Section 16 of the EIAO. Reference sections
in the EIAO-TM provide the details of the assessment criteria and guidelines that are
relevant to the water quality assessment, including:
• Annex 6 - Criteria for Evaluating Water Pollution
• Annex 14 - Guidelines for Assessment of Water Pollution
Water Pollution Control Ordinance (WPCO)
The WPCO provides the major statutory framework for the protection and control of
water quality in Hong Kong. According to the Ordinance and its subsidiary legislation,
Hong Kong waters are divided into ten Water Control Zones (WCZs). Corresponding
statements of Water Quality Objectives (WQOs) are stipulated for different water
regimes (marine waters, inland waters, bathing beaches subzones, secondary
contact recreation subzones and fish culture subzones) in the WCZs based on their
beneficial uses. According to Item 3.5.5.2 of the Study Brief, the assessment area
for this water quality impact assessment covers the Deep Bay WCZ as designated
under the WPCO. The WQOs for the watercourses in the Deep Bay WCZ relevant
to the water quality impact assessment are listed in Table 5.1.

Technical Memorandum for Effluents Discharged into Drainage and Sewerage
Systems, Inland and Coastal Waters (TM-DSS)
Discharge of effluents is subject to control under the WPCO. The TM-DSS gives
guidance on the permissible effluent discharges based on the type of receiving waters
(foul sewers, storm water drains, inland and coastal waters). The standards control
the physical, chemical and microbial quality of effluents. The discharge limits vary
with the effluent flow rates and the effluent should comply with the standards for
effluent discharged into inland waters for irrigation, pond fish culture or amenity
subject to the exact locations. The TM-DSS also specifies the discharge standards
into foul sewers leading into the Government's sewage treatment plants. Subject to
the flow rate of the effluents, corresponding standards for the effluent discharge into
the Government's foul sewers should be followed.

Professional Persons Environmental Consultative Committee Practice Notes
(ProPECC PNs)
A ProPECC PN was issued by the EPD to provide guidelines for handling and
disposal of construction site discharges. The ProPECC PN 2/24 "Construction Site
Drainage" provides good practice guidelines for dealing with 10 types of discharge
from construction sites. These include surface run-off, groundwater, boring and
drilling water, wastewater from concrete batching and/or precast concrete casting,
wheel washing water, bentonite slurry, water for testing and/or sterilisation of water
retaining structures and water pipes, wastewater from building constructions, acid
cleaning, etching and pickling wastewater, and wastewater from site facilities.
Practices given in the ProPECC PN 2/24 should be followed as far as possible during
construction to minimise the water quality impact due to construction site drainage.
The ProPECC PN 1/23 "Drainage Plans Subject to Comment by the EPD" provides
guidelines and practices for handling, treatment and disposal of various effluent
discharges to stormwater drains and foul sewers during the operation phase. The
design of site drainage and disposal of various site effluents generated within the new
development area should follow the relevant guidelines and practices as given in the
ProPECC PN 1/23.
Environment, Transport and Works Bureau Technical Circular (ETWB TC)
ETWB TC (Works) No. 5/2005 “Protection of natural streams/rivers from adverse
impacts arising from construction works” provides an administrative framework to
better protect all natural streams/rivers from the impacts of construction works. The
procedures promulgated under this Circular aim to clarify and strengthen existing
measures for protection of natural streams/rivers from government projects and
private developments. The guidelines and precautionary mitigation measures given
in the ETWB TC (Works) No. 5/2005 should be followed as far as possible to protect
the inland watercourse at or near the Project area during construction phase.
Hong Kong Planning Standards and Guidelines (HKPSG)
Chapter 9 of the HKPSG outlines environmental requirements that need to be
considered in land use planning. The recommended guidelines, standards and
guidance cover the selection of suitable locations for the developments and sensitive
uses, provision of environmental facilities, and design, layout, phasing and
operational controls to minimise adverse environmental impacts. It also lists out
environmental factors that influence land use planning and recommends buffer
distances for land uses.

Shenzhen River (S1) locates at the northern portion of assessment area. It is a
channelised watercourse which generally flows from northeast to southwest and
finally enters the marine water of Deep Bay WCZ. It is the drainage outlet of Ng Tung
River, Ping Yuen River and the San Tin streams on Hong Kong side. It has been
straightened, widened and deepened to improve its flood prevention level. Tidal
influence occurs along the entire Shenzhen River.
LMC Meander (S2) is the largest natural watercourse in the northern portion of
assessment area. S2 was originally part of Shenzhen River and was restored to
mitigate the loss of fish ponds from training of the Shenzhen River. Water in S2 is
upstream of Shenzhen River which originates from adjacent hillside at the southern
portion of assessment area and therefore the water quality was less polluted
compared to Shenzhen River. Tidal influence was observed occasionally according
to the water quality monitoring results as stated in Section 5.3.3.
S3 and S4 are small natural watercourses in Tai Law Hau and Ping Hang respectively.
These watercourses are upstream tributaries of the LMC Meander (S2), which
originate from adjacent hillside at the southern portion of assessment area, flow from
south to north and lead northward to S2. As mentioned in Section 5.3.3, although
stagnant and turbid water was observed at during low water flow condition in dry
season, the water quality of S4 is generally good.
S5 is a small natural watercourse in Tse Koo Hang. It originates from adjacent hillside
at the southern portion of assessment area, flows from south to north, runs through
the farmlands and villages in Tse Koo Hang and finally discharges to the wet
grassland/marsh/ponds in Ma Tso Lung.

Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -

Ma Tso Lung Nullah/Stream (S6) was a natural stream before 2008 and was trained
as a drainage nullah under the project 4156CD - Drainage improvement in Ki Lun
Tsuen, Ma Tso Lung, Ying Pun, Shek Tsai Leng and Sha Ling in New Territories.
Upstream of S6 is a natural stream near the Ma Tso Lung Shun Yee San Tsuen. As
mentioned in Section 5.3.6, the water quality of S6 is excellent with limited
contamination by organic and nutrient pollutants.
S7 is a small natural watercourse near Ma Tso Lung Shun Yee San Tsuen. This
watercourse is upstream tributaries of Ma Tso Lung Nullah/Stream (S6) which
collects surface runoff from nearby local villages and nature hillsides, passing through
a pond and marsh and finally joins S6.
S8 are several small natural watercourses which collects surface runoff from adjacent
hillside (including Crest Hill), flows to Liu Pok at the east and finally discharges to the
wet grassland/marsh/ponds in Ta Sha Lok.
A continuous pond area was recorded at Ma Tso Lung, Hoo Hok Wai area and
adjacent to Lok Ma Chau Meander (P2 and P3). Majority of the ponds recorded in
P2 and P3 are fishponds. Several small ponds (P1, P4, P5, P6) were identified within
the assessment area which scattered in the area near Ma Tso Lung Shun Yee San
Tsuen, Tse Koo Hang, Ping Hang and Tai Law Hau. These ponds are located near
village areas and are inactively managed by nearby villagers, or abandoned.
The Project site is located within the Wetland Conservation Area (WCA) and Wetland
Buffer Area (WBA).
Conservation area (CA) is also identified within the assessment area. CA is
designated as conservation area under the Approved Lok Ma Chau Loop Outline
Zoning Plan (OZP) No. S/LMCL/2, Approved Ma Tso Lung and Hoo Hok Wai OZP
No. S/NE-MTL/3 and Approved San Tin Technopole OZP No. S/STT/1 to cover the
LMC Meander and the wetland and fish ponds which form an integral part of the
wetland ecosystem at Hoo Hok Wai and Deep Bay area.
Ecological Area (EA) is identified within the assessment area. EA was created along
the southeastern edge of the Loop, covers an area of approximately 12.78 ha to
compensate for the loss of wetland habitats due to the Loop’s development (register
no.: AEIAR-176/2013).
Assessment Methodology
The Project falls within the Deep Bay WCZ as designated under the WPCO (Cap.
358). The assessment area should include areas within 500m from the boundary of
the Project and its associated works as identified in the EIA Study. The WSRs in the
vicinity of the Project have been identified. Potential sources of water quality impact
that may arise during the construction and operation stages of the Project were
described, including point discharges and non-point sources to surface water runoff,
sewage from workforce and polluted discharge generated from the Project. All the
identified sources of potential water quality impact at the identified WSRs were
evaluated and their impact significance determined with reference to the WQOs or
criteria covered in Annex 6 and 14 of the EIAO-TM. Practical water pollution control
measures were recommended to mitigate identified water quality impacts.

Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
Identification, Prediction and Evaluation of Environmental Impacts
Construction Phase
General construction works for the Project would be land-based only and within the
Project site. The potential sources of water quality impact associated with the land-
based works would include:
• Construction works in LMC Meander and EA;
• Wastewater from general construction activities;
• Construction site run-off;
• Construction works near watercourses;
• Diversion of watercourse;
• Removal of ponds and wet areas;
• Accidental spillage of chemicals;
• Sewage from construction workforce; and
• Groundwater infiltration arising from formation of underpass/depressed road.
Construction Works in LMC Meander and EA
Underpass road will be constructed across the LMC Meander and EA. Excavation
works will be required during cut-and-cover underpass road construction in the LMC
Meander and EA, which may lead to elevated suspended solids (SS) levels and
dispersion of SS to the downstream Shenzhen River/Deep Bay waters if in contact
with waters in the Meander and EA.
To separate the construction works from the meander and EA, cofferdams will be
used to enclose the excavation works. The construction of underpass road across
the LMC Meander will be divided into two stages (half width of the Meander per each
stage). Details on construction of cut-and-cover underpass enclosed by cofferdams
are discussed in Section 2. Water pumps will be used to collect any construction site
runoff and ingress/seepage water within the cofferdams. The collected construction
site runoff and ingress/seepage water will be diverted to the on-site wastewater
treatment facilities for treatment to satisfactory levels before discharge. Silt curtains
shall be deployed to completely enclose the cofferdams prior to setting up excavation
works, and installation of cofferdams. Silt curtains shall only be removed after
completion of cut-and-cover construction works, and removal of cofferdams. The
riverbed of the LMC Meander (section for underpass road) and EA will be reinstated
upon completion of the Project.
Excavated materials (including sediment) may be generated from the construction
works in the LMC Meander and EA. Mitigation measures for handling and disposal of
excavated materials and sediment as recommended in Section 5.7.25 should be
followed to minimise the potential environmental impacts arising from the excavated
materials.

Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
The construction of underpass road across the LMC Meander will be conducted by
phases and only one cofferdam will be installed in each stage. Since the cross-
section area of the LMC Meander to be blocked by the cofferdams is anticipated to
be localised and temporary, the change in flow regime would be localised and any
local water quality impact would expect to be transient. As a result, the potential
impact on water quality and hydrology of the LMC Meander and EA would be
insignificant, no adverse water quality would be expected if the mitigation measures
detailed in Sections 5.7.1 to 5.7.4 are implemented properly.
Construction Site Runoff and Wastewater from General Construction Activities
Wastewater generated from construction activities, including general cleaning and
polishing, wheel washing, dust suppression and utility installation may contain high
SS concentrations and a certain amount of grease and oil. Wastewater may also be
generated from the accumulation of solid waste such as debris, rubbish, plastic
package and construction materials. Sediment laden run-off during site formation
works, if uncontrolled, may carry pollutants (absorbed onto the particle surfaces) into
the nearby water bodies. Potential pollution sources of site run-off may include:
• Run-off and erosion of exposed bare soil and earth, drainage channel, earth
working area and stockpiles;
• Release of any bentonite slurries, concrete washings and other grouting
materials with construction run-off or storm water;
• Wash water from dust suppression sprays and wheel washing facilities; and
• Fuel, oil and lubricants from maintenance of construction vehicles and
equipment.
During rainstorms, site run-off would wash away the soil particles on unpaved lands
and areas with the topsoil exposed. The run-off is generally characterised by high
concentration of SS. Release of uncontrolled site run-off would increase the SS levels
and turbidity in the nearby water environment. Site run-off may also wash away soil
particles that were contaminated by the construction activities and therefore cause
water pollution.
Wind-blown dust would be generated from exposed soil surfaces in works areas. It is
possible that wind-blown dust would fall directly onto the nearby water bodies when
a strong wind occurs. Dispersion of dust within the works areas may increase the SS
levels in surface run-off causing a potential impact to the nearby sensitive receivers.
It is important that proper site practice and good site management be followed to
prevent run-off with high level of SS from entering the surrounding waters. Best
Management Practices (BMPs) in controlling construction site discharges are
recommended for this Project as described in Sections 5.7.5 to 5.7.18. In view of
the sensitive nature of the Deep Bay WCZ, an Emergency Response Plan (ERP)
should also be developed to minimise the potential impact from construction site
discharges under failure of treatment facilities during emergency situations or
inclement weather. An outline of the ERP is provided in Sections 5.7.34 to 5.7.35.
With the implementation of BMPs to control construction site effluents and ERP to
minimise water quality impact under emergency situations, disturbance of water
bodies would be avoided and deterioration in water quality would be minimal.

Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
Construction Works near Watercourses
Watercourses were identified within the Site as identified in Section 5.4.
Construction works in close proximity to the inland watercourses may pollute the
inland waters due to potential release of construction wastes and wastewater.
Construction wastes and wastewater are generally characterised by high
concentration of SS and elevated pH. Adoption of good housekeeping and mitigation
measures would reduce the generation of construction wastes and potential water
pollution. The implementation of measures to control run-off and drainage water will
be important for the construction works adjacent to the inland water in order to prevent
run-off and drainage water with high levels of SS from entering the water environment.
With the implementation of BMPs as described in ProPECC PN 2/24 "Construction
Site Drainage" and provision of mitigation measures as specified in ETWB TC (Works)
No. 5/2005 "Protection of natural streams / rivers from adverse impacts arising from
construction works" (also see Sections 5.7.5 to 5.7.19), it is anticipated that water
quality impacts would be minimised.
Diversion of Watercourse
Temporary diversion will be required during cut-and-cover construction of depressed
road across Ping Hang Stream (S4). Diversion of watercourse would involve
excavation and construction works for diverting the water flow from the existing route
to the temporary drainage system. Potential impacts may be generated by release
of construction materials, wastewater, excavated sediment, spillage and
contaminants to the receiving waters in the downstream (due to soil excavation for
construction of temporary drainage). All these construction works should be
undertaken in dry conditions to avoid potential water quality impacts upon the
downstream water quality.
The tentative works sequence for diversion of watercourse should be duly planned to
minimise water quality impacts as described below. A temporary drainage at most
downstream should first be established to intercept and divert the upstream flow. The
temporary drainage should be constructed and completed before dewatering of the
existing watercourse. Construction of the temporary drainage should be undertaken
in a dry condition prior to receiving any water flow. Precautionary measures in
Appendix D of ETWB TC No. 5/2005, such as temporary isolation to other connected
watercourse using sandbags and silt curtains, should be used to isolate the works
areas from neighbouring waters. Dewatering of watercourse should be performed by
diverting the water flow to temporary drainage. Silt removal facilities should be
adopted to treat the wastewater from dewatering operations prior to discharge.
Construction works at watercourse should be undertaken only after dewatering
operation is fully completed to avoid water flow in the works area. After completion
of the construction works, the works area shall be cleaned up before receiving any
water flow or connecting to any existing watercourse.
Excavated materials (including sediment) may be generated from the diversion of
watercourse. Mitigation measures for handling and disposal of excavated materials
and sediment as recommended in Section 5.7.25 should be followed to minimise the
potential water quality impacts arising from the excavated materials.
Mitigation measures for protection of downstream water quality from diversion of
watercourses are described in Sections 5.7.20 to 5.7.23. With adoption of the
recommended mitigation measures, no adverse water quality impacts are anticipated.

Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
Removal of Ponds and Wet Areas
Three ponds (P2) will be drained during construction and integrated into enhanced
wetland after completion of works. Partial area of wet grassland (in WBA) in between
the Tse Koo Hang Stream (S5) and WCA will also be removed under this Project.
All the affected ponds and wet areas should be isolated and not connected to any
existing watercourse. The associated construction works would include draining the
water in ponds and wet areas before filling up these areas or before commencement
of any excavation and construction works. The water of these ponds and wet areas
to be drained would probably be sediment-laden and would carry a certain level of
pollutants. Direct dumping of these drained waters to the nearby watercourse will not
be allowed.
The drained water generated from dewatering of the ponds/wet areas to be removed
should be temporarily stored in appropriate storage tanks or containers for reuse on-
site as far as practicable and any surplus water should be tankered away for disposal
at the Sewage Treatment Works (STW). Any surplus water should be treated as
necessary before disposal to the STW in compliance with the TM-DSS. In order to
minimise the potential impact, dewatering works at ponds and wet areas should be
conducted within dry season to minimise the quantity of drained water. No direct
discharge of drained water from these construction works will be allowed.
Excavated materials (including sediment) may be generated from the construction
works in ponds and wet areas. Mitigation measures for handling and disposal of
excavated materials and sediment as recommended in Section 5.7.25 should be
followed to minimise the potential water quality impacts arising from the excavated
material. Together with the adoption of the mitigation measures for removal of ponds
and wet areas as recommended in Sections 5.7.24, no adverse water quality impact
would be expected.
Accidental Spillage of Chemicals
The use of engine oil and lubricants and their storage as waste materials have the
potential to create impacts on the water quality if spillage occurs. Waste oil may
infiltrate into the surface soil layer, or runoff into adjacent waterbodies, increasing
hydrocarbon levels. Groundwater pollution may also rise from the improper use and
storage of chemical and petroleum products within the site area where groundwater
infiltrates into the area. Infiltration of groundwater may occur at areas where there are
faults and/or fissures in the rock mass. The potential impacts could however be
mitigated by practical mitigation measures and good site practices (as given in
Sections 5.7.26 to 5.7.28).
Sewage from Construction Workforce
During the construction of the Project, the workforce on site will generate sewage
effluents, which are characterised by high level of BOD, ammonia and E. coli.
According to Table T-2 of “Guidelines for Estimating Sewage Flows for Sewage
Infrastructure Planning” (GESF), the unit flow factor (UFF) is 0.23 m3/day/employee
(0.08 m3/day/employee for commercial employee and 0.15 m3/day/employee for
employees of construction activities). For every 100 construction workers working
simultaneously at the construction site, about 23 m3 of sewage would be generated
per day. Potential water quality impacts upon the local drainage and fresh water
system may arise from these sewage effluent, if uncontrolled.

Groundwater Infiltration arising from Formation of Underpass/Depressed Road
The underpass / depressed road will be constructed by cut-&-cover method which
may result in infiltration of groundwater. The major concern of groundwater infiltration
from the underpass/depressed road construction activities would be the increase in
site runoff and the associated potential drawdown of groundwater in any soil and
aquifer layers. Infiltrated water would carry away silt from site into the site drainage
and any potential drawdown of groundwater would result in different degrees of
settlement and dewatering of surface water features. Consideration should be taken
in the underground structure design to minimise the infiltration of groundwater. With
the implementation of the recommended groundwater control/mitigation measures as
described in Section 5.7.31 to 5.7.33, the potential groundwater infiltration would be
minimised and no adverse water quality impact would be anticipated.

• Non-point source surface runoff from new impervious areas.

Surface runoff to be generated from the Project site is known as non-point source

Project site could be washed into the nearby drainage system or even into the
watercourses during rainfall event. Surface runoff generated from the paved or
developed areas may contain debris, refuse and dust. Practices that cleaning agents
used for road washing may also affect the water quality of the nearby receiving water.

Construction Site Runoff and General Construction Activities
Control of potential pollution of nearby water bodies during the construction phase of
the Project should be achieved by measures to:
• prevent or minimise the likelihood of pollutants (generated from construction
activities) being in contact with rainfall or run-off; and
• abate pollutants in the stormwater surface run-off prior to the discharge of
surface run-off to the nearby water bodies.
These principle objectives should be achieved by implementation of the Best
Management Practices (BMPs) of mitigation measures in controlling water pollution.
The guidelines for handling and disposal of construction site discharges as detailed
in the ProPECC PN 2/24 "Construction Site Drainage" should be followed, where
applicable. All effluent discharged from the construction site should comply with the
standards stipulated in the discharge licence under the WPCO. The following

and when properly implemented should be sufficient to adequately control site
discharges so as to avoid water quality impacts.
Construction Site Runoff
Surface run-off from construction site should be discharged into storm water drains
via adequately designed on-site wastewater treatment facility such as sand traps, silt
traps, sedimentation tanks and sediment basins. Channels, earth bunds or sand bag
barriers should be provided on site to properly direct surface run-off to such silt
removal facilities. Perimeter channels at site boundaries should be provided where
necessary to intercept surface run-off from outside the site so that it will not wash
across the site. Catchpits and perimeter channels should be constructed in advance
of site formation works and earthworks.
Silt removal facilities, channels and manholes should be maintained and the
deposited silt and grit should be removed regularly, at the onset of and after rainstorm
to ensure that these facilities are functioning properly at all times. Before disposal at
the public fill reception facilities, the deposited silt and grit should be solicited in such
a way that it can be contained and delivered by dump truck instead of tanker truck.
Any practical options for the diversion and realignment of drainage should comply
with both engineering and environmental requirements in order to provide adequate

Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
Construction works should be programmed to minimise soil excavation in the rainy
seasons (generally from April to September). If soil excavation cannot be avoided in
these months or at any time of year when rainstorms are likely, for the purpose of
preventing soil erosion, temporarily exposed slope surfaces should be covered (e.g.
by tarpaulin), and temporary access roads should be protected by crushed stone or
gravel, as excavation proceeds. Intercepting channels should be provided (e.g. along
the crest / edge of excavation) to prevent surface run-off from washing across
exposed soil surfaces. Arrangements should always be in place to ensure that
adequate surface protection measures can be safely carried out well before the
arrival of rainstorm.
Earthworks final surfaces should be well compacted and the subsequent permanent
work or surface protection works should be carried out immediately after the final
surfaces are formed to prevent erosion caused by rainstorms. Appropriate drainage
like intercepting channels should be provided where necessary.
Measures should be taken to minimise the ingress of rainwater into trenches. If
excavation of trenches in the rainy season is necessary, they should be dug and
backfilled in short sections of length. Rainwater pumped out from trenches or
foundation excavations should be discharged into storm drains via silt removal
facilities.
Open stockpiles of construction materials (e.g. aggregates, sand and fill material) on
sites should be covered with tarpaulin or similar fabric during rainstorms. Measures
should be taken to prevent the washing away construction materials, soil, silt or debris
into any drainage system.
Manholes (including newly constructed ones) should always be adequately covered
and temporarily sealed so as to prevent silt, construction materials or debris from
getting into the drainage system, and to prevent storm run-off from getting into foul
sewers. Discharge of surface run-off into foul sewers must always be prevented in
order not to unduly overload the foul sewerage system.
Boring and Drilling Water
Water used in ground boring and drilling for site investigation or rock/soil anchoring
should as far as practicable be re-circulated after sedimentation. When there is a
need for final disposal, the wastewater should be discharged into storm drains via silt
removal facilities.
Wheel Washing Water
